text.p: In overnight commodity markets, copper prices bounced slightly after their sharp dive of the first three days of the week, but their US$25 a tonne rise appeared unconvincing, traders said.
Oil prices dropped back as traders took a second look at the OPEC deal struck on Wednesday.
Gold prices edged slightly higher, but continue to lanquish around four year lows set in February.
Wheat rose on U.S. export news and a harvest slowdown,
The CRB index closed down 2.31 points at 239.40.
Copper prices were sent back under the $2,400 a tonne level during late Thursday LME ring and kerb trading, although the market still concluded the session higher.
Traders said the market's gains today were little more than a technical reaction to oversold momentum indicators after the sell-offs seen earlier this week.
Prices were unable to clear resistance around $2,415, and the subsequent slippage under $2,400 suggests that the seven-weeks lows of $2,355 hit yesterday are likely to come under attack again.

Market sentiment is likely to be influenced by rising stocks, with a 1,625-tonne increase today in LME warehouse inventories -- the fourth successive daily rise -- taking the running total this week to 3,200 tonnes.

Given the stock increases, which show signs of becoming the norm, and the summer slowdown, the market might now be tilting into surplus and so has little more scope on the upside. Last trade was at $2,398 a tonne, well down from the high, but still $25 up from Wednesday's kerb close.

Aluminium was steadier, but was unwilling to tackle the resistance between $1,580 and $1,600. However, falling stocks and forward consumer interest should restrict dips, as they did on Wednesday. Last business was at $1,577 a tonne, up $8 from the previous kerb.

Zinc notched up a fresh near-seven year high during the afternoon, building on the strong raly from sub-$1,400 levels seen on Wednesday. Last business was at $1,412, up $16. Nickel prices remained above the support band pegged around $7,000/7,030, although market movements were inhibited by the lack of news from the Inco talks at Sudbury.
Talks resumed on Wednesday, but there have been no developments reported. Last trade was at $7,070, up $20 from Wednesday.

An OPEC deal to freeze quotas has dodged the thorny issue of overproduction and papered over the cracks in the cartel's leaky quota system, oil traders said on Thursday. The deal would do little to stem downward pressure on oil prices despite insistence by the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) that quota-busting by its members had been addressed, they added. Oil prices slid steadily lower on

Thursday after the deal was struck and many dealers saw the chance of further losses. Brent blend crude oil futures, the world benchmark grade, closed down 37 cents at $17.85 a barrel but were still well above a recent 12-month low of $17.32.

COMEX and NYMEX precious metals futures ended mixed Thursday, on moderate volumes, with gold finding some support, after weakness earlier in the month. In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $338.00/50, compared to the London Thursday afternoon fix at $336.95 an ounce, and the New York close
Wednesday around $337.10/60, and not far from the four year low at $336.90 on February 12.

CBOT soft red winter wheat futures closed higher on export news and a harvest slowdown, traders said. U.S. exporters on Thursday said Pakistan bought 500,000 tonnes of wheat with 350,000 of the tally coming from the U.S. Also overnight, Paris-based sources said Algeria bought roughly 275,000 tonnes of wheat, one-half came from the U.S. Activity in the U.S. Great Plains wheat harvest region found favor with wheat bulls. Wheat
closed one to 3-3/4 cents per bushel higher, with July up 1-1/4 at $3.33 a bushel and September closed three cents higher at $3.43.

CSCE world July sugar futures settled tightly mixed as a three-day speculative buying spree came to a close, market sources said. The spot July contract ended down 0.04 cent at 11.11 cents per lb, traded 11.19 to 11.10 cents.
